text: Come, let us sing for joy to the LORD; let us shout aloud to the rock of our salvation.
Let us come before him with thanksgiving, and shout to him with songs of praise.
For the LORD is a great God, a great King above all gods.
In his hand are the depths of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his.
The sea is his, for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.
Come, let us worship and bow low; let us kneel before the LORD our Maker.

versions.text: Come, let us bow down in worship, let us kneel before the LORD our Maker.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew stacks three distinct verbs of reverence (prostrate oneself, bow down, kneel). The current rendering collapses the first two into one phrase; keeping all three preserves the cumulative, rhythmic build of the call to worship.

text: For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, the flock under his hand. Today, if only you would listen to his voice!

Do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, as on that day at Massah in the wilderness,[^1]

[^1]: Meribah means "quarreling" and Massah means "testing"; the place names echo the accusation being made.

versions.text: Do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, as on that day at Massah in the wilderness,
versions.explanation: The place names carry meanings that are essential to the verse's wordplay with the following line ("your ancestors tested me"). A brief footnote helps hearers catch the connection without altering the readable text.

text: where your ancestors tested me; they tried me, though they had seen what I did.
For forty years I loathed that generation, and I said, "They are a people whose hearts go astray; they have not known my ways."

versions.text: For forty years I was angry with that generation, and I said, "They are a people whose hearts go astray; they have not known my ways."
versions.explanation: The verb here denotes disgust or loathing rather than simple anger; using "loathed" also avoids repeating "anger" in the very next verse, where a different Hebrew word (nostril/wrath) is used.

versions.text: For forty years I loathed that generation,
versions.explanation: More than half the Hebrew verse is missing: וָאֹמַר עַם תֹּעֵי לֵבָב הֵם וְהֵם לֹא־יָדְעוּ דְרָכָי ("and I said, 'They are a people whose hearts go astray; they have not known my ways'"). The dropped clause is essential — it supplies the reason for the oath in verse 11 — and the current text also ends with a comma leading nowhere. The verb "loathed" from the intentional earlier revision is retained.

text: So I swore in my anger, "They shall never enter my rest."
